newsitem.title: USA: Police on lookout for rebel supporters in Texas.
newsitem.headline: Police on lookout for rebel supporters in Texas.

text.p: Police were on the lookout on Thursday for a caravan of recreational vehicles said to be carrying reinforcements for armed Texas separatists holed up in a remote mountain compound.

Fears that supporters of the Republic of Texas group were coming to the rugged Davis Mountains of west Texas prompted a security clampdown in which state troopers searched cars near the compound and in this village nearly 20 miles (32 km) away.

Dozens of heavily-armed police and 13 Republic members have been in a tense standoff since Sunday when the separatists, who advocate Texas' secession from the United States, took two hostages in a hail of gunfire. The hostages were later released, but felony charges were filed against the rebels.

Trooper John Barton of the Texas Department of Public Safety told Reuters police got a report late on Wednesday that a caravan of three "RVs" and other vehicles carrying Republic supporters from Arkansas was within 200 miles (321 kilometres) of Fort Davis.
"We alerted all state troopers to be on the lookout," he said, but the group, which supposedly said it was on a fishing trip to New Mexico, had not been located.
He said there were reports of other groups planning to help the Republic of Texas, but nothing confirmed. "We're asking them to stay back, stay back," Barton said.

Seven men said to be Republic supporters were arrested on Wednesday at a truck stop in Pecos, Texas, about 70 miles (112 km) north of Fort Davis. Their two cars were loaded with guns, supplies and thousands of rounds of ammunition, police said.

The fear that the standoff could become a rallying point for anti-goverment militia groups has forced the usually rough-and-tumble Texas police to take uncharacterstically gentle measures to extract the rebels from their hideout.
Telephone negotiations with rebel leader Richard McLaren nearly produced a surrender early on, but on Tuesday night he suddenly stopped talking and has been silent ever since.
"We would like for him to try and contact us," Barton pleaded.
"Maybe the raccoons have eaten through the telephone line," quipped McLaren's attorney, Terence O'Rourke, as he tried to put a positive spin on his client's silence.

Police tried to restart talks by rumbling up to the compound in a 13-ton armoured personnel carrier to drop off a "diplomatic pouch" with messages from police and O'Rourke asking McLaren to call or send back his response in the pouch.
There had been no reply by midnight on Wednesday so police planned to repeat the operation on Thursday.

Barton said they were also stepping up the pressure by cutting off power to the ramshackle compound that McLaren calls "the embassy" for his erstwhile republic. He described the move as "routine procedure...non-violent and non-threatening."

The Republic of Texas group, formed in 1995, believes the 1845 annexation of Texas by the United States was illegal. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after breaking away from Mexico in 1836.
